summary: A mid-fourteenth-century great helm surviving with its heraldic crest — one of the very few medieval crests to come down to us at all.
details: Crests were made of light perishable materials and almost none survive. This one does, which turns a rare object into a uniquely informative one.
knownFor: One of the very few medieval helms to survive with its crest.
Albert von Prankh’s seal of 1353 carries the same two-horned crest, tying the object to the man.
Hung for centuries in the church at Seckau, beneath two Prankh funerary shields.
Felt-lined reinforces over the face — tournament equipment rather than battlefield.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: This is a great helm of about the middle of the fourteenth century, associated with the Prankh family of Styria, and it survives with something almost nothing else does: its heraldic crest.

Great helms themselves are rare but not unique. Crests are a different matter — they were built of light, perishable materials precisely so they could be worn on the head, and virtually none have come down to us.
The result is an object that answers a question the written and painted record leaves open: what a crest was actually like as a physical thing, rather than as a device drawn on a page.

contentSections.title: Date and provenance
paragraphs: The helm is dated to roughly 1330 to 1350 and is associated with Albert von Prankh, of a Styrian family within the Holy Roman Empire.

The link between man and object is better founded than tradition. Albert’s seal survives on a document of 1353 and shows two horns with combs closely matching the crest on this helm — independent evidence tying the heraldry to the person.

It comes from a church rather than a battlefield or a grave. It hung for centuries high on the wall of the southern aisle at Seckau in Styria, beneath two Prankh funerary shields, and was taken down in 1877 and presented to the imperial collections in Vienna the following year.

contentSections.title: Construction
paragraphs: The helm is the classic fully enclosing form: an iron vessel covering the whole head and resting on the shoulders, with a narrow vision slit and breathing holes, in the shape that dominates knightly imagery of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries.
Above it rises the crest — a pair of horns springing from a fanned base, finished in gilding and silvering, so that the whole assembly would have flashed in sunlight at a distance.

The crest is not iron. Medieval crests were made from light materials such as leather, parchment, cloth and wood over a frame, because a heavy one would have been unwearable, and it is exactly that lightness which normally guarantees they do not survive.

contentSections.title: Attribution and reliability
paragraphs: The association with Albert von Prankh is unusually well founded for an object of this kind: a known family, a known church, a documented removal in 1877, and a seal of 1353 whose crest matches the one on the helm.

What is less certain is the relationship between the helm and any fighting he did. The reinforcing plates over the face, lined with felt, point to the hastilude — the tournament melee — rather than to war, and the helm carries cuts on every side.

Albert himself is barely recoverable. He is known essentially through that seal and through this helm, and there is not enough surviving record to write a life. This archive therefore names him without linking to a biography it cannot responsibly write, rather than manufacturing a thin one to satisfy a cross-link.

contentSections.title: Historical context
paragraphs: The great helm existed because a closed face solved one problem and created another: a man inside one could not be recognised, so he had to be identified by display. Crest, shield and surcoat carried the same arms for that reason.

This helm was probably not battlefield equipment. Its felt-lined face reinforces belong to the hastilude, the mock battle in which knights fought in teams with lance, sword and mace, and the marks on it are consistent with that.
The date fits. By the middle of the fourteenth century the great helm was already giving way to the bascinet in war, and its continued life belonged to the tournament and to ceremony.

contentSections.title: The surviving object today
paragraphs: It is held by the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna, in the Hofjagd- und Rüstkammer, among the most important collections of arms and armour in the world.
It is displayed with the crest in place, which is how it should be seen — helm and crest were designed as one visual object and neither makes full sense alone.
Its condition reflects centuries hanging in a church rather than use: the iron is worn and the crest's finish is degraded, but the assembly is intact.

contentSections.title: Significance
paragraphs: It is the best surviving answer to what heraldry looked like in three dimensions. Coats of arms are abundantly documented on parchment and stone; the objects themselves are almost entirely gone.

It also demonstrates why funerary achievements matter to arms history out of proportion to their number. The Black Prince's achievements at Canterbury survive for the same reason, and between them these objects preserve a class of material that ordinary use destroyed.
For the archive it is a reminder that the most informative surviving objects are frequently not the ones that saw the most fighting, but the ones that were taken out of use and hung somewhere safe.
